svg.text: Why the network terminates in the FPGA — taking the operating system off the boundary
Same UTL-X guard, two ways to connect it. The difference is what untrusted bytes touch first, and who controls the interlink if software is compromised.
Network through the processor — the "normal" way
the operating system sits ON the boundary
untrusted bytes hit millions of lines of OS code
the attacker owns the network stack AND decides what goes over the interlink.
Network through the FPGA — the UTL-X Guard design
no operating system on the boundary: the boundary is a circuit
• size and rate limits at line rate
• no TCP/IP, ARP, ICMP, no open ports
OS network stack — not on the boundary
no ports, no ping, no ARP — only DMA buffers
Every point where data enters or leaves is a small, fixed circuit fixed by a signed bitstream —
even a fully compromised Linux cannot change what the FPGA accepts or what it sends over the interlink.
First code that untrusted bytes touch
OS kernel: drivers, ARP, ICMP, TCP/IP — millions of lines
no — protocol break, payload only via DMA
after the OS has buffered the data
FPGA stays transmit-only; side B verifier rejects
deterministic circuit with a fixed function

Figure — Network termination in the FPGA removes the operating system from the boundary: untrusted traffic meets a fixed circuit, and the interlink is controlled by hardware, not software (illustrative).
